what_it_measured.text: The atherosclerotic plaque area in aortic sinus and arch, plasma lipid profile, fatty acid composition, hepatic enzyme activities and gene expression were determined.

We investigated a salmon protein hydrolysate (SPH) that is hypothesized to influence lipid metabolism and to have anti-atherosclerotic and anti-inflammatory properties. 24 female apolipoprotein (apo) E−/− mice were divided into two groups and fed a high-fat diet with or without 5% (w/w) SPH for 12 weeks.

endpoint.text: A blinded operator to the study quantified plaque area, extracellular matrix and lipid deposition, as well as inflammatory cell infiltrate.
An operator blinded to dietary treatment quantified the atherosclerotic plaques.

reported_results.text: A significantly reduced atherosclerotic plaque area in the aortic arch and aortic sinus was found in the 12 apoE−/− mice fed 5% SPH for 12 weeks compared to the 12 casein-fed control mice.
A significant reduction in lesion area was observed at the aortic sinus of mice fed SPH compared to controls (1.27±0.41×105 μm2 vs. 2.02±0.31×105 μm2; Fig. 2A–C).

A significantly lower plaque development was observed in the aortic arch in SPH-fed mice compared to control mice (0.55±0.33 vs. 1.63±0.99×106 μm2; Fig. 1, corresponding to 0.91±0.55 vs. 2.72±1.72% of the aortic surface covered by plaque).
At sacrifice, the average weight gain was 5.98±1.78 g (mean ± SD) in controls and 5.04±0.88 g in SPH mice (P>0.05).
Results The SPH-diet Decreased Atherosclerotic Plaque Development After 12 weeks on a high-fat diet, 5% SPH-fed mice displayed a weight gain similar to the control group.
We showed that apoE−/− mice fed a high-fat diet containing 5% (w/w) SPH for 12 weeks developed less atherosclerotic plaques compared to controls.
